newsitem.title: USA: State Department blasts Cuba on bomb charges.
newsitem.headline: State Department blasts Cuba on bomb charges.

text.p: State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns on Monday blasted Cuba for making what he said were unsupported charges that people in the United States were behind the bombing of two hotels in Havana at the weekend.

He also derided Cuba for withdrawing at the last minute from a series of baseball games with the United States, saying what leader Fidel Castro really feared was the prospect that players would defect to a better life in the United States.
Two small bombs exploded within minutes of each other on Saturday in the lobbies of the Hotel Nacional and Hotel Capri, slightly injuring three people and causing minor damage.
A brief Interior Ministry statement said the ministry had evidence to show the people responsible for the bombs and the material used were from the United States. The ministry gave no other details.
"There's no evidence whatsoever that Americans were behind it. And needless to say, the United States government had absolutely nothing to do with this," Burns told reporters.

"If there's any information the Cuban government has that they think is real and they want to turn it over to us, if they think Americans are implicated, we will listen. But there's no evidence. There's no information," he said.
"The Cuban government has launched a serious charge against Americans. It better put up or shut up," he added.
Asked if Cuba might have reason to feel threatened because of the history of some hardline anti-Castro groups among the Cuban exile community in Miami, Burns exploded:
"In our country ... if you want to indict somebody or indict a whole group of people, an entire ethnic group in our country, then you better have your facts straight."
Some of these exile groups have carried out violent action in the past, or have threatened to do so.

Florida is a key state in U.S. presidential politics and the Cuban-American community there is a powerful political force. The United States has no diplomatic relations with the Communist regime in Havana and the Clinton administration has fanned hostility between the two capitals to a fever pitch.
Burns accused Cuba of being "paranoid...They've got a failed system."

Earlier on Monday, Cuba withdrew at the last minute from a series of baseball games against the United States, citing fears for the safety of players and saying one reason for the cancellation was the weekend bombing of two Havana hotels.
A statement by the Cuban national sports body INDER said conditions for the eight-game series, which was to start in Norwich, Connecticut, on Tuesday, were "not favourable for our team."
Burns said the idea that Cuban players might feel threatened walking the streets of Norwich -- a small city -- "is a little bit strange."

"Now, what he's (Castro) probably most afraid of is that, because they come from a Stalinist society, because he keeps them down on the farms literally and doesn't allow them to earn what they're worth in the free market, he's afraid that most of these players or a great number of them are going to walk. And they're going to defect to the United States."
Burns, an obsessive baseball fan, said "we would gladly welcome more Cubans pitching and playing ball in the American League."
